chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
We generate freight revenues by transporting products from our three commodity groups. Freight revenues vary with volume (carloads) and average revenue per car (ARC). Changes in price, traffic mix, and fuel surcharges drive ARC. Customer incentives, which are primarily provided for shipping to/from specific locations or based on cumulative volume, are recorded as a reduction to operating revenues. Customer incentives that include variable consideration based on cumulative volume are estimated using the expected value method, which is based on available historical, current, and forecasted volume, and recognized as the related performance obligation is satisfied. We recognize freight revenues over time as shipments move from origin to destination. The allocation of revenues between reporting periods is based on the relative transit time in each reporting period with expenses recognized as incurred.
Other subsidiary revenues (primarily logistics operations) are generally recognized over time as shipments move from origin to destination. The allocation of revenues between reporting periods is based on the relative transit time in each reporting period with expenses recognized as incurred. Accessorial revenues are recognized at a point in time as performance obligations are satisfied.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Freight revenues increased 15% in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025 driven by higher fuel surcharge revenues, 6% carload growth, and core pricing gains, which more than offset an unfavorable business mix (from an increase in shipments with lower ARC, such as intermodal). Higher intermodal shipments, which increased 11% in the third quarter compared to one year ago, combined with strong metals and minerals, energy and specialized markets, and grain and grain products shipments were partially offset by lower coal shipments. Year-to-date 2026 freight revenues increased 10% compared to 2025 due to higher fuel surcharge revenues, 3% volume growth, and core pricing gains, partially offset by business mix (from increased intermodal shipments). Higher grain and grain products, intermodal, metals and minerals, and industrial chemicals and plastics shipments more than offset lower coal and automotive shipments.
Each of our commodity groups includes revenues from fuel surcharges. Freight revenues from fuel surcharge programs increased to $1.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026 compared to $602 million in the same period of 2025 due to higher fuel prices and increased volume.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Other subsidiary revenues increased in the third quarter of 2026 compared to 2025 due to higher demand for shipments at our subsidiary that brokers intermodal and transload logistics services, partially offset by lower revenues from the sale of a portion of revenue-generating assets in late 2025 from our technology subsidiary. Additionally, in the year-to-date period, other subsidiary revenues were negatively impacted from the transfer of commuter operations to Metra. Accessorial revenues increased in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by higher container, intermodal accessorial, and demurrage revenues.

Bulk – Bulk includes shipments of grain and grain products, fertilizer, food and refrigerated, and coal and renewables. Freight revenues from bulk shipments increased 10% in the third quarter of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by higher fuel surcharge revenues and core pricing gains on essentially flat volume. Lower wheat and soybean meal volume, lower coal shipments due to low natural gas prices and elevated plant inventories, and lower fertilizer shipments offset continued export grain strength in addition to higher renewable fuels, ethanol, and associated feedstock shipments. For the year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025, freight revenues from bulk shipments increased 9% from higher fuel surcharge revenues, 3% volume growth from higher grain and grain product shipments, and core pricing gains, partially offset by business mix (from lower food and refrigerated carloads).

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text: Industrial – Industrial includes shipments of industrial chemicals and plastics, metals and minerals, forest products, and energy and specialized markets. Freight revenues from industrial shipments increased in the third quarter and year-to-date of 2026 compared to 2025 due to increased volume, core pricing gains, and higher fuel surcharge revenues, partially offset by business mix (from higher plastics and rock shipments). While all industrial business teams contributed to the 6% volume increase for the third quarter of 2026 compared to 2025, increased domestic steel, construction project-related material, and plastics demand in addition to business development efforts for higher petroleum and lumber shipments primarily drove the growth. Year-to-date carloads improved 4% as increased demand for industrial chemicals and plastics and construction project-related materials coupled with business development efforts, more than offset reduced soda ash export shipments.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text: Premium – Premium includes shipments of finished automobiles, automotive parts, and merchandise in intermodal containers, both domestic and international. Premium freight revenues increased 21% and 12%, respectively, in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by higher fuel surcharge revenues, volume growth, and core pricing gains, partially offset by business mix (from higher intermodal shipments). In the third quarter of 2026, intermodal volume increased 11% with continued strong domestic intermodal growth driven by business development and reduced truck market capacity, as well as, higher international intermodal carloads due to improving U.S. West Coast import volume and business development efforts. In addition, automotive shipments improved 2% in the third quarter of 2026 due to higher auto parts shipments resulting from business development efforts. Year-to-date 2026 intermodal volume increased 2% compared to 2025 as a 13% increase in domestic intermodal shipments more than offset a 12% decline in international intermodal carloads as a result of elevated U.S. West Coast imports in the first half of 2025. Automotive shipments decreased 1% in the year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 from lower production as a result of weaker finished vehicle demand, which offset business development efforts.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations

Mexico business – Freight revenues from each of our commodity groups includes revenues from shipments to and from Mexico, which increased 9%, to $820 million, in the third quarter of 2026 driven by fuel surcharge revenues and 4% volume growth from increased intermodal, finished vehicles, and construction-related shipments, partially offset by lower grain and forest product shipments. For the year-to-date period of 2026, Mexico freight revenues increased 7% to $2.4 billion compared to 2025 driven by higher fuel surcharge revenues and volume growth. Increased intermodal, finished vehicles, and grain products shipments more than offset lower petroleum, auto parts, beverage, and metals shipments, resulting in 4% volume growth.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text: Fuel – Fuel includes locomotive fuel and gasoline for highway and non-highway vehicles and heavy equipment as well as the associated taxes and transportation costs. Fuel expense increased in both the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to the same periods in 2025 driven by higher locomotive diesel fuel prices and increased gross ton-miles, partially offset by improvement in the fuel consumption rate (computed as gallons of fuel consumed divided by gross ton-miles in thousands), which improved 2% in both respective periods. Locomotive diesel fuel prices averaged $4.21 and $3.59 per gallon in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026, respectively, compared to $2.56 and $2.49 per gallon in the corresponding respective periods of 2025.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Purchased services and materials – Expense for purchased services and materials includes the costs of services purchased from outside contractors and other service providers (including equipment maintenance and contract expense incurred by our subsidiaries for external transportation services); materials used to maintain the Railroad’s lines, structures, and equipment; costs of operating facilities jointly used by UPRR and other railroads; transportation and lodging for train crew employees; trucking and contracting costs for intermodal containers; leased automobile maintenance expense; and tools and supplies. Purchased services and materials increased 9% in the third quarter and year-to-date period of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by higher subsidiary and intermodal volume-related costs and inflation. For the third quarter of 2026, lower acquisition-related costs more than offset the increased costs associated with maintaining a higher active fleet. Year-to-date, increased acquisition-related costs contributed to a portion of the year-to-date expense increase.
Depreciation – The majority of depreciation expense relates to road property, including rail, ties, ballast, and other track material. Depreciation expense increased 4% for both the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by a higher depreciable asset base.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text: Equipment and other rents – Equipment and other rents expense primarily includes rental expense that the Railroad pays for freight cars owned by other railroads or private companies; freight car, intermodal, and locomotive leases; and office and other rent expense, offset by equity income from certain equity method investments. Equipment and other rents expense decreased 3% and 6%, respectively, in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by lower operating equipment lease expense and lower car hire expense from shorter haul length and volume-related incentives. These declines were partially offset by increased demand in business (primarily intermodal and construction project-related materials) utilizing freight cars owned by others and favorable 2025 contract settlements. Year-to-date, improved cycle times also contributed to lower equipment and other rents expense, although it was partially offset by lower equity income compared to 2025.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Other – Other expense includes state and local taxes; freight, equipment, and property damage; utilities; insurance; personal injury; environmental remediation; employee travel; telephone and cellular; computer software; bad debt; and other general expenses. Other expense increased 1% and 5%, respectively, in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by higher environmental and destroyed equipment casualty costs and other general expenses, which were partially offset by lower personal injury costs, property tax expense, and bad debt expenses. The year-to-date period of 2026 was also impacted by higher damaged freight costs.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Gross and revenue ton-miles – Gross ton-miles are calculated by multiplying the weight of loaded and empty freight cars by the number of miles hauled. Revenue ton-miles are calculated by multiplying the weight of freight by the number of rate miles. Gross ton-miles increased 4% while revenue ton-miles increased 5% in the third quarter of 2026 compared to 2025 and corresponding carloads increased 6%. For the year-to-date period of 2026 compared to 2025, gross ton-miles increased 3% and revenue ton-miles increased 5% while corresponding carloads increased 3%. The variance in gross ton-miles, revenue ton-miles, and carloads was driven by changes in business mix. In the third quarter of 2026, business mix was impacted by higher intermodal shipments, which are generally lighter, while the year-to-date business mix was affected by higher grain shipments that are generally heavier.
Freight car velocity – Freight car velocity measures the average daily miles per car on our network. The two key drivers of this metric are the speed of the train between terminals (average train speed) and the time a rail car spends at the terminals (average terminal dwell time). Freight car velocity increased 1% and 5%, respectively, in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 driven by reduced terminal dwell combined with improved train speed in both periods.
26
Table of Contents

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Locomotive productivity – Locomotive productivity is gross ton-miles per average daily locomotive horsepower available. In the third quarter of 2026, locomotive productivity remained consistent with 2025 as the active fleet increased 2% to support 4% higher gross ton-miles while maintaining network fluidity and asset efficiency. For the year-to-date period, locomotive productivity improved 2% compared to 2025, with a 1% smaller active fleet handling 3% more gross ton-miles.
Train length – Train length is the average maximum train length on a route measured in feet. Train length increased 2% in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 due to train length improvement initiatives, including optimization of the transportation plan and mainline capacity investments, enabling us to efficiently handle increasing carload volume.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Service performance index (SPI) – SPI is a ratio of the service customers are currently receiving relative to the best monthly performance over the last three years. Measuring our performance relative to a historical benchmark demonstrates our focus on continuously improving service for our customers. Our SPI is calculated for intermodal and manifest products. For the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026, both SPI measures declined compared to the respective 2025 period as a result of a comparison against a higher benchmark standard. Intermodal SPI declined 6 points and 2 points, respectively, in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026 compared to 2025 while manifest SPI declined 7 points and 3 points, respectively.
Workforce productivity – Workforce productivity is average daily car miles per employee. Workforce productivity improved 5% in the third quarter and year-to-date periods of 2026, respectively, compared to 2025. Lower employee levels, which declined 1% and 3%, respectively, combined with higher average daily car miles enabled the improvement. We continually align our active train, engine, and yard (TE&Y) workforce to meet customer demands while operating a fluid network.

chunks.heading: Item 2. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
chunks.text:
Operating ratio – Operating ratio is our operating expenses reflected as a percentage of operating revenues. For the third quarter of 2026, our operating ratio of 59.1% improved 0.1 points as top-line growth from increased volume and core pricing gains, productivity, and lower acquisition-related costs offset the impact of higher fuel costs and inflation. The year-to-date 2026 operating ratio of 59.7% deteriorated 0.1 points as the impact of higher fuel prices, inflation, and acquisition-related expenses more than offset core pricing gains, productivity initiatives, and the positive comparison from the $55 million crew staffing agreement ratification charge in 2025.

Capital plan
In 2026, we expect our capital plan to be approximately $3.5 billion. We plan to continue to make investments to support our growth strategy, improve the safety, resiliency, and operational efficiency of the network, harden our infrastructure, and replace older assets, including modernization of our locomotive fleet and acquiring freight cars to support replacement and growth opportunities. In addition, the plan includes investments in growth-related projects to drive more carloads to the network and enhance productivity through technology. This includes terminal investments supporting our manifest network and intermodal ramps to efficiently handle new and existing customers, along with siding investments (extensions and new), and second mainline track projects. The capital plan may be revised if business conditions warrant or if laws or regulations affect our ability to generate sufficient returns on these investments.
